beats.title: A guaranteed market for a new seed
beats.body: In 1966 India imported 18,000 tonnes of Mexican dwarf wheat seed, with Ludhiana among the trial sites. Around the seed, the state built a market: regulated mandis (1961), the Food Corporation of India and a prices commission (1965), and a support price, wheat at Rs 54 a quintal in 1966–67.
beats.today: The guaranteed price and government purchase still decide what Punjab plants.
beats.source: Lok Sabha answer, 1982; Punjab Agricultural Produce Markets Act, 1961; Food Corporations Act, 1964; CACP.

beats.title: Rice comes to a wheat state
beats.body: Paddy covered about 285,000 hectares of Punjab in 1966–67, and 1.18 million by 1980–81: four times as much in fourteen years. It is transplanted into standing water in June, in the heat before the monsoon, so it is watered from the ground.
beats.today: Paddy covers about 3 million hectares, ten times the 1966 area.
beats.source: P. Singh & R. R. Singh, The Tribune, 2017; R. S. Ghuman (CRRID), The Tribune, 2018.

beats.title: Wells everywhere, and a fight over the power bill
beats.body: Electric tubewells spread across the fields: about 6 lakh by 1980–81. In 1983 the Bharatiya Kisan Union told farmers to stop paying their electricity bills, and in March 1984 they besieged the Governor's House in Chandigarh on tractor trolleys, demanding cheaper power and better crop prices. Operation Blue Star that June silenced the movement for a decade.
beats.today: What a farmer pays to pump became a political question, not an economic one.
beats.source: S. S. Gill, Journal of Sikh & Punjab Studies 29, 2022; R. S. Ghuman, The Tribune, 2018.

beats.title: Free power, endless pumping
beats.body: From January 1997, electricity for farm tubewells was free. With no cost for each hour of pumping, nothing on a farmer's bill says when to stop.
beats.today: Farm power is still free; the state budgets about Rs 10,000 crore a year for it (2025–26).
beats.source: The Tribune, 2025; well depths: CGWB monitoring wells (bottom right).

beats.title: Chasing the water down
beats.body: As the water fell, farmers drilled deeper and swapped surface pumps for submersibles. NASA's GRACE satellites found the aquifers under Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan losing about 18 cubic kilometres of water a year between 2002 and 2008. In 2009 Punjab passed a law barring paddy transplanting before a set date in June, to save water.
beats.today: The law still sets the planting dates each year.
beats.source: Rodell, Velicogna & Famiglietti, Nature, 2009; Indian Ecological Society, 2025; Punjab Preservation of Subsoil Water Act, 2009.

beats.title: The ground sinks, the fire moves
beats.body: Later transplanting means a later harvest and less time before wheat, so the stubble is burned in late October and November, when the air is still. Satellites also measure the land itself sinking as the aquifer empties.
beats.today: 81 fires detected over the belt between 1 October and 3 November 2026.
beats.source: Agarwala, Bhattacharjee & Dasgupta, Ashoka University WP 61; Scientific Reports, 2022; InSAR study of Ludhiana, 2024; NASA FIRMS (own count).

beats.title: Defending the guarantee
beats.body: In September 2020, three farm laws opened crop trade outside the regulated mandis. Punjab's farmers read them as the first step towards ending guaranteed purchase, and camped at Delhi's borders for a year until the laws were repealed in November 2021.
beats.today: The system holds. All 11 blocks of the belt pump more water than returns to the ground each year, and paddy still earns Rs 2,441 a quintal.
beats.source: Gazette of India; CGWB 2025–26 via INGRES; paddy MSP 2026 as reported.
